# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles population series for 1.200 urban centres, garrison foundations (*amsar*), fortified towns (*kastra*) and caravan stations across 24 modern national jurisdictions from 632AD to 1000AD. Drawn from six archaeological and historical-geographical registers after excluding 250 subordinate suburbs, duplicate aliases and superseded entries, the dataset tracks 881 active centres housing 5,74M inhabitants in 632AD, 1.194 centres housing 8,41M by 650AD, 1.196 centres housing 9,03M at the 850AD Abbasid peak and 1.194 centres housing 9,28M in 1000AD. Grouped into six geographic divisions covering Iraq and al-Jazira, Bilad al-Sham and Cyprus, Egypt, Iran and Afghanistan, Byzantine Anatolia and Caucasia, and North Africa with the Arabian Peninsula, the tables show how Rashidun garrison foundations (Basra, Kufa, Fustat, Kairouan), Umayyad market towns (Wasit, Ramla) and Abbasid river capitals (Baghdad, Samarra, Raqqa) reshaped older Late Antique urban networks without extinguishing classical Mediterranean or Iranian oasis cities [@Nol2023Arab; @Bessard2018Politics; @ALJabri2023Developmen; @Bosworth2007Historic].



# Background

Urbanism across the Early Islamic Caliphate and its Byzantine and Caucasian frontiers was neither a sterile preservation of Hellenistic civic geometry nor an abrupt collapse into nomadic pasture. Between 632AD and 1000AD, old Roman, Byzantine and Sassanid cities coexisted with planned Muslim foundations whose street grids, congregational mosques, *suq* market halls and waterworks answered fiscal and military imperatives [@Allahham2025Untold; @Yassin2012Architectu; @Bessard2018Politics]. In Iraq and Egypt, the Rashidun conquests immediately generated purpose-built garrison camps (*amsar*) at Basra (638AD), Kufa (638AD) and Fustat (641AD), followed in Ifriqiya by Kairouan (670AD) [@Nol2023Arab; @ALJabri2023Developmen; @Bosworth2007Historic]. Positioned along navigable river margins or desert-steppe interfaces where tribal cavalry could assemble without billeting inside existing civic quarters, these camps quickly grew into permanent craft and trading cities sustained by *kharaj* grain and silver stipends [@Yuksel2024Mecca; @Isoldi2026Confluent].

Under the Umayyad caliphs (661AD to 750AD), planned foundations multiplied across Syria, Palestine and lower Mesopotamia. Governors laid out Wasit (702AD) as a Syrian-garrisoned administrative bridge between Kufa and Basra, while Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik established al-Ramla (c. 715AD) as the provincial capital of Jund Filastin, displacing coastal Caesarea without erasing inland market towns such as Jarash, Tiberias and Damascus [@Nol2021Defining; @Stern2025Mamluk; @Ali2026Dimensions]. The Abbasid transfer of the seat of power to Iraq in 750AD shifted metropolitan gravity east again. Al-Mansur's Round City of Baghdad (762AD) and al-Mu'tasim's palace-garrison belt at Samarra (836AD) towered over the Tigris corridor, supported by the dense canal networks of the Sawad [@ALJabri2023Developmen; @Wahhab2024Decorative]. Further east, Samanid and Buyid patronage turned Nishapur, Rayy, Shiraz, Merv and Balkh into high-density *qanat*-fed manufacturing metropolises on the Silk Roads [@Saatsaz2023Technology; @Lu2023Connected; @Michailidis2014Dynastic]. Meanwhile, in Byzantine Anatolia, seventh-century raids compressed open *poleis* into fortified hilltop *kastra* such as Amorium, Ancyra and Anazarbos before ninth- and tenth-century frontier stability renewed provincial towns [@Coleman2021Poleis; @Bakirtzis2023Introducin; @Navruz2024Historical].

# Methodology

The 1.200 settlement entries tabulated here represent the vetted core of 1.450 candidate records compiled for HANDBOOK between 632AD and 1000AD. Candidate locations and occupation intervals were cross-matched across the Pleiades Ancient World Gazetteer (839 entries), the Al-Thurayya Early Islamic Gazetteer (382 entries), the Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire (171 entries), the Published Excavations Atlas (87 entries), the Egypt Exploration Society Delta Survey Gazetteer (2 entries) and the C-Turkey Chronometric Register (1 entry), with foundation chronologies and Islamic historical toponyms cross-checked against Bosworth's urban reference volume [@Bosworth2007Historic] strictly as a supplemental gazetteer alongside primary morphological and archaeological literature [@Nol2021Defining; @Mokranova2025Material; @Mitchell2021Church]. Out of 1.450 candidates, 250 were excluded prior to tabulation to prevent spatial double counting: 155 subordinate suburbs merged into metropolitan cores, 86 lower-priority duplicates superseded by primary registers and 9 alias variants.

Settlement names preserve scholarly Latin transliteration matching Cornu-Romanov and Pleiades conventions, while modern national jurisdictions follow current boundaries across 24 states to allow direct comparison with modern geoBoundaries subadministrative units [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries]. Coordinates are reported in decimal degrees (European comma notation) alongside each site's active chronological span inside the 632AD to 1000AD window. Benchmark population estimates appear at 632AD (the Prophet's death), 850AD (the Abbasid peak) and 1000AD (the turn of the millennium); periods before foundation or after abandonment are marked with a hyphen (-).

# Testing and Validation

Across all 1.200 catalogued urban centres, log-log rank-size regression yields a Zipf exponent $\alpha = 0,283$ ($R^2 = 0,666$), displayed in Figure \ref{fig:settlements-gazetteer}. Mean settlement size rises modestly from 6.515 inhabitants across 881 active centres in 632AD to 7.042 across 1.194 centres in 650AD, 7.549 across 1.196 centres in 850AD and 7.776 across 1.194 centres in 1000AD. As discussed in the companion regional study, the shallow Zipf slope reflects HANDBOOK's tiered urban scaling ceiling - which caps primary metropolises at 44.519 and secondary regional seats at 17.808 to 18.000 - to prevent unverified literary population claims from distorting continuous Matérn kriging densities.

# Results

## Al-Iraq and Al-Jazira

## Bilad al-Sham and Cyprus

Table \ref{tab:zone2-sham} records 162 settlements across Syria, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Cyprus and Palestine, including Umayyad Damascus, Aleppo (*Halab*), Raqqa, Antioch, al-Ramla and Gerasa, reflecting dense urban-rural commercial continuity across the Levant [@Bessard2018Politics; @Nol2021Defining; @Mokranova2025Material; @Stern2025Mamluk].

## Iran, Khorasan and Afghanistan

Table \ref{tab:zone4-iran} covers 193 settlements across Iran and Afghanistan, including Shiraz, Hamadan, Nishapur, al-Ahwaz, Ardabil, al-Sirjan, Shahrastan, Rayy, Tus, Siraf, Balkh, Herat and Marw al-Rudh, anchoring *qanat*-irrigated oasis agriculture and Silk Road craft manufacture [@Saatsaz2023Technology; @Lu2023Connected; @Michailidis2014Dynastic; @Spooner2019Epilogue].

## Byzantine Anatolia and Caucasia

Table \ref{tab:zone5-anatolia} enumerates 260 centres across Turkey, Georgia, Azerbaijan and Armenia, spanning fortified Byzantine *kastra* and *Thughur* border cities (Ancyra, Tarsus, Anazarbos, Amid, Cnidus, Phocaea, Ani) as well as Constantinople's Marmara frontier and Transcaucasian valley towns [@Coleman2021Poleis; @Mitchell2021Church; @Bakirtzis2023Introducin; @Ozbal2026Diet].

## North Africa and the Arabian Peninsula

# Limitations

Three constraints qualify individual settlement entries in this gazetteer. First, the maximum population tier is capped at 44.519 in 1000AD across eleven leading metropolises, with secondary provincial capitals clustered near 17.808 to 18.000 and smaller fortified centres near 6.431 to 6.500; users seeking literary estimates of Abbasid Baghdad's peak intramural and suburban population must treat these values as spatial-model tier weights rather than absolute headcounts [@ALJabri2023Developmen; @Bosworth2007Historic]. Second, spatial site density is highest in Anatolia, Egypt, Syria and Iraq where Pleiades, DARE and Al-Thurayya coverage overlap, and thinner in interior Arabia, desert Libya and central Afghanistan. Third, several classical monuments or wall segments retained in Pleiades (such as gates of Nineveh or city walls of Anazarbos and Ani) stand in as coordinate proxies for persistent early mediaeval urban nuclei rather than isolated fortifications.

# Conclusion

Taken together, the 1.200 catalogued settlements demonstrate broad continuity and selective restructuring across the Early Islamic world and Byzantine Anatolia between 632AD and 1000AD. Active urban and fortified sites expanded from 881 centres housing 5,74M inhabitants in 632AD to 1.194 centres housing 9,28M by 1000AD, driven by the seventh-century *amsar* wave, Umayyad foundation towns in Syria and Palestine, Abbasid metropolitan growth along the Tigris and resilient oasis urbanisation across Iran, Khurasan, Egypt and the Maghrib.
